10772-inca-land-explorations-in-the-high:
Hiram Bingham, the Yale explorer, published Inca Land in 1922 about his explorations in the highlands of Peru. Chapters cross deserts, climb Coropuna, visit Lake Titicaca and the Vilcanota country, and search for the last Inca capital. The fortress of Uiticos, the house of the Sun, Vilcabamba, and the pampa of ghosts mark the trail.

Bingham writes of the last four Incas and their mountain refuge, quoting Kipling's explorer as his motto. His narrative mixes adventure with archaeology, as ruins and valleys yield their secrets. Readers get a classic of exploration, from the man who brought the Inca highlands to world fame.
1209-history-of-the-conquest-of-peru:
William Hickling Prescott, the blind Boston historian, tells how Francisco Pizarro, with a handful of Spaniards, overthrew the Inca Empire in the 1530s. The narrative follows the march to Cajamarca, the capture of Atahualpa, the ransom of gold, and the civil wars that followed among the conquerors.

Prescott writes with a storyteller's sweep, drawing on Spanish chronicles and judging both Inca and Spaniard with care. The history made his fame, and it remains a classic of narrative history. Readers meet a tale of courage, greed, and ruin on a grand scale.
12961-the-dock-and-the-scaffold-the-manc:
The Dock and the Scaffold tells the Manchester tragedy of November 23, 1867, and the cruise of the Jacknell, in a partisan Irish nationalist voice. Dawn crowds fill Manchester's frosty streets as the city wakes to an execution day, with burghers, children, and hurrying throngs pouring through dim lanes. Moore's God Save Ireland verses frame the tale.

Later passages give prisoners' speeches from the dock, protesting false witnesses, blood money, and alibis that juries would not hear. One man notes a policeman who swore to a prisoner arrested two days later. The book stands as a vivid, one-sided record of the Fenian executions and their aftermath.
19318-the-outdoor-girls-in-the-saddle-or:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this 1922 Outdoor Girls tale, In the Saddle, or the girl miner of Gold Run. Betty, Grace, Mollie, and Amy plan a ranch adventure. Betty is the Little Captain. The girls argue their parents around to letting them use a wild ranch. Fur leggings, sombreros, Indians, and broncho busters fill their talk.

Betty beams that the girls are the whole show. Grace raves it would be heavenly to ride all day. Mollie asks impatiently whether it is really certain they will get the chance. A girl miner at Gold Run waits ahead. Young readers get a lively girls' western of horses, ranch life, and friendship.
21061-under-the-chilian-flag-a-tale-of-w:
Harry Collingwood set this sea tale in the war between Chile and Peru in the late 1870s, fought over a desert rich in nitrates. Two young Englishmen serve aboard the Pericles, a British steamer carrying nitrates, silver ore, and hides between Chilean ports and Liverpool. Their captain is so unpleasant that they decide to leave him.

Short of officers, the Chilean navy takes the two men on. What follows tracks their adventures and hardships in Chilean service during the war. Spanish ship names and local words colour the action. The result is a boys' naval story built on a real South American conflict.
21066-harry-escombe-a-tale-of-adventure-:
Harry Escombe works as a young draughtsman in a civil engineer's office. His firm wins a contract to survey and build a railway in Peru. Harry is picked to go, and success there could make his future. The man in charge of the project, though, is a deeply nasty character.

That chief sends Harry on a needlessly risky survey, and Harry falls from a cliff and is given up for dead. He survives in a coma, wakes among local people, and is taken for a returned Inca god. Worshipped in their city, he must somehow escape and find his way home to England.
26602-an-account-of-the-conquest-of-peru:
Pedro Sancho, secretary to Pizarro and scrivener to his army, wrote this account of the conquest of Peru. Philip Ainsworth Means translated it into English and annotated it for the Cortes Society at New York in 1917. The edition was limited to 250 copies. Means calls it among the most valuable accounts of the conquest, rich in ethnological detail on the Inca dominion at its fall.

Means also warns readers that the narrative is an apologia for Pizarro, inspired by Pizarro himself to restore his favor with the emperor and to answer his enemies' charges. The original manuscript is lost, surviving through Ramusio's Italian Viaggi of about 1550 and Icazbalceta's Mexico edition of 1849. Chapters cover Cuzco gold and silver, the royal fifth, Caxamalca, and the capture of Atabalipa.
3453-the-royal-road-to-health-or-the-sec:
Tyrrell offers a health manual from the early twentieth century that promises health without drugs. The book argues that much sickness comes from waste and impurity held inside the body. It sets out a daily system of diet, water, and internal cleanliness meant to keep the body clear. Its tone is confident and practical, aimed at ordinary readers rather than doctors.

Readers today should treat the claims as period advice, not as modern medicine. The book's interest lies in what it shows about health fads of its time. Those fads mixed distrust of patent medicines, faith in simple habits, and a belief that nature could cure what drugs could not. It is a window into popular health writing before modern science reshaped the field.
686-the-treaty-of-the-european-union-maa:
The full text of the treaty signed at Maastricht on 7 February 1992, which set up the European Union. It records the member states recalling the end of Europe's division and their wish to build firmer bases for a shared future. It states their bond to liberty, democracy, respect for human rights, and the rule of law.

The treaty sets out aims for closer union while respecting each people's history, culture, and ways of life. It covers deeper bonds between peoples, shared action abroad, and stronger common work at home. As a source text, it matters because it is the founding act itself, not a summary: readers can see the exact pledges and terms on which the Union was built.
7070-the-treasure-of-the-incas-a-story-o:
G A Henty builds The Treasure of the Incas on a mystery never fully cleared: the loss of a large part of the Inca treasure. Spaniards tortured the natives trusted with the secret and made two or three finds, but those were likely a small share of the missing hoards. For years after occupation, Spaniards spared no pains and no cruelty to bring hidden wealth to light.

The story of a boat that put to sea laden with treasure is historical, and most supposed she was lost in a storm soon after sailing. It was also morally certain that Peruvians leaving when Spaniards became masters carried off much wealth. An illustration shows sacks swiftly transferred into a boat. Henty turns that mystery into a boys quest in Peru.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-jose-urr:
Juan José Urraburu was a Basque Jesuit philosopher of the Scholastic revival. Born at Ceánuri in Biscay in 1844, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1860 and taught rhetoric, philosophy, and theology. In 1878 he was called to Rome to teach philosophy at the Gregorian University for nine years. He later led colleges at Valladolid, Oña, and Salamanca.

Urraburu's eight-volume Institutiones philosophiae, published from 1890 to 1900, covers logic, ontology, cosmology, psychology, and natural theology. His five-volume Compendium became the textbook of Jesuit houses in Spain and beyond. Critics received his work with care and favor, and his influence spread widely in his order. He died at Burgos in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lima-peru:
Lima, in its namesake department, is the capital of Peru. After the sixteenth-century conquest of the Incas, Pizarro chose a site about 600 feet above sea level and laid the cathedral's first stone on 18 January 1535. Lima became a diocese in 1543 and an archdiocese in 1545 under the Dominican Loaysa, its first bishop and archbishop. St. Torribio Mogrovejo succeeded him and died of fever caught visiting and baptizing Indians.

The University of San Marcos was founded at Lima in 1551, the first in the New World. The Jesuits arrived in 1567 and brought schools and the printing press. Its harbour at Callao, nine miles away, made it the centre of Spain's trade monopoly until Utrecht in 1713. Riva Agüero became first president in 1823. In the war with Chile, Lima fell on 14 January 1881. Its national library became a barrack, and books were destroyed or sold as waste paper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuel-de-men:
Manuel de Mendiburu was a Peruvian soldier, statesman, and historian, born at Lima in 1805 and dead there in 1885. He studied at San Marcos under Javier de Luna Pizarro and became an amanuensis of the Consulate in 1819. At independence he joined the army as ensign, rose under San Martin to lieutenant, fought at Calana, Locumba, Torata, and Moquegua, and was captured and freed by Spaniards.

 He governed several departments as prefect, directed Lima's School of Arts and Trades from 1870, and held the portfolios of agriculture, foreign affairs, war, and marine. He sat in the Chamber of Deputies, led the army as general-in-chief, and served as envoy to Britain, Bolivia, and Chile. His life's work, the Diccionario historico-biografico del Peru, records Peruvians who served their country, from Inca times through the colonial age. He also rebuilt Lima's library and national archives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peru:
Peru was a South American republic on the Pacific coast, founded in 1821 after its war of independence from Spain. This long Catholic Encyclopedia survey opens with the name itself. Most writers trace it to native words like Beru, Pelu, and Biru. The land covers 679,000 square miles between Ecuador and Chile, cut from south-east to north-west by the Andes. Religion runs through the whole story.

Spanish conquest and mission marched together, the entry argues, from papal sanction and crown orders for conversion to the missionaries who trailed the soldiers. Later sections follow colonial rule, independence, government, and the Church's dioceses, schools, and missions among native peoples. Gold drew the conquerors, but the narrative keeps faith beside greed as the twin motor of Peru's founding.
doe-osti-17120805-fy27-final-report-work: Nuclear inspectors compared notes in FY27, and this report captures the safeguards workshop. The pages log the talks and lessons. The inspectors get their record. The record was FY27. The lessons were logged. The notes were compared. The inspectors got records.
doe-osti-3028866-an-educational-guide-fo: ESTER got educationally guided, and this DOE guide calculates rotating stars. The pages detail the 2D findings. The educators get their data. The stars were rapidly rotating. The data were educator. The ESTER were code. The rotating were rapidly. The 2D were calculations.
doe-osti-3375579-strong-shaktoolik-batte: Shaktoolik got battery-constructed, and this DOE text covers the system project. The pages detail the construction findings. The energy folks get their data. The project was construction. The data were energy. The Shaktoolik were battery. The construction were project.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingMartinLuthe:
Henry P. Leifermann reported for United Press International from Memphis on an unusual demand. Humbert James Putt, a federal prisoner, insisted on testifying in the trial of James Earl Ray. A court had ruled Putt mentally incompetent. His claims touched both the King and Kennedy assassinations, and the wire described them as bizarre.

Big cases attract claimants from every margin, and Ray's trial drew its share. A prisoner demanding the stand with tales of two assassinations tested the court's patience and the wire's restraint. Leifermann's report preserves the episode as Memphis read it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MullenRobertRud:
Ron Rosenbaum wrote 'Wallowing in Watergate' about a document the Ervin Committee never released. The committee's staff had prepared a 46-page study of connections between Howard Hughes and Larry O'Brien. O'Brien chaired the Democratic National Committee, whose headquarters were burgled in the Watergate break-in. The study was deleted from the committee's output.

Rosenbaum asks why a finished staff study on Hughes and O'Brien was buried. Hughes money moved through the politics of both parties, and O'Brien had worked for Hughes. The article follows the deleted study as a story inside the larger scandal: work done, then suppressed, then reported on anyway. It is Watergate told through one missing document.
history-of-the-conquest-of-peru:
William Hickling Prescott's History of the Conquest of Peru appears here without the footnotes of its companion edition. It opens by ranking Peru with Mexico as Spanish adventure's most brilliant passages. His preface describes writing nearly blind. He dictated from notes and composed on a frame made for the blind. Its characters looked like hieroglyphics his secretary learned to read.

The narrative covers the Inca empire's polity, Pizarro's expeditions, the capture of Atahuallpa, and the civil wars of the conquerors. The Inca, reverenced as more than human, ruled thoughts as well as conduct in Prescott's account. Despite his eyesight, the American historian built from Spanish archives a narrative still read for its sweep and sympathy.
lenin-development-capitalism-russia-1899:
Lenin wrote The Development of Capitalism in Russia in 1899, signing it with the name Vladimir Ilyin. The Russian original is the text held here. Narodnik writers had claimed that capitalism could not take root in peasant Russia. Lenin answers them with a mass of Russian statistics.

He shows markets, wage labor, and class splits already growing inside the village. That evidence formed the empirical base of Russian Marxism. The book grew from his Siberian exile studies and prison work. No public domain English translation exists, so the Russian stands alone. Readers with Russian meet the young Lenin as researcher. The data tables fill many pages.
nasa-tm-19660021939-application-of-a-dou:
S S Manson, J C Freche, and C R Ensign at Lewis Research Center applied a new fatigue rule in a paper for a crack meeting in Atlantic City in mid 1966. Parts under repeated load fail in two stages: a crack first forms, then it grows. Their double linear damage rule treats the two stages apart, each with its own straight-line damage count. Steel fatigue tests judge the rule.

Forecasting fatigue life decides when parts must be retired. A rule that fits both stages should forecast better than a single-line rule. Turbine and airframe parts live under exactly such repeated loads. The authors test their rule against real steel data, in a symposium devoted to crack growth, where rival methods met the same evidence.
nasa-tm-19680025225-the-solar-constant-a:
Goddard Space Flight Center teams measured the solar constant and solar spectrum from a research aircraft in August 1967, as this August 1968 report records. The NASA 711 Galileo experiment flew at about 38,000 feet. Flying high cut the air above the instruments, sharpening sunlight measurements. Matthew P. Thekaekara served as principal investigator for one interferometer instrument.

Dwight C. Kennard Jr. managed the project, with Raymond Kruger coordinating at Ames Research Center. Instruments included interferometers, a cone radiometer, and a filter radiometer. Charles H. Duncan and James J. Webb led thermophysics branch experiments. The report documents the flight program and its instrument teams. Precise solar output values anchor climate science and spacecraft thermal design.
nasa-tm-19690031067-seasonal-transitions:
J. S. Theon and W. S. Smith of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this September 1969 preprint, numbered X-621-69-393. They tracked seasonal transitions in the mesosphere's thermal structure at high latitudes. Acoustic grenade experiments, flown from Barrow, Alaska, timed sound echoes to profile middle air temperatures through the turning seasons.

Winter's disturbed features appeared high in the mesosphere in September, the pair report. Month by month they reached successively lower altitudes, until the full winter pattern stood by December. Then an early January warming at the stratopause began reversing the whole structure. That chain of events would in time restore the calm summertime case. Their watch ran from September 1968 through February 1969, catching both transitions.
nasa-tm-19720015325-spaceport-news-index:
The Kennedy Space Center Library issued this index on April 3, 1972, as report GP-969. Mrs Olive C Ankersen of the Documents Department compiled it. The index covers Spaceport News, the center's own newspaper. Its span runs from December 1962 through February 1972. Those years carried Kennedy from early Mercury work through the Apollo landings. The library aimed to capture that march of events for reference.

The index serves as a ready tool for finding names, places, and events. Together they make up the history of the Kennedy Space Center. Entries sit in alphabetical order by subject. Under each subject, the matching news items follow. Staff and historians could trace a person or program quickly. The foreword frames indexing as preserving history, not mere filing.
podcast-tuckercarlson-DPPla5e_fRU:
Tucker Carlson opens with the last scene of Orwell's Animal Farm. Pigs and men play cards together, hard to tell apart. He uses the image to judge the MAGA movement's fate.

The title warns of snakes in Washington warping the movement's meaning. Carlson argues leaders who once claimed rebellion now serve power. He asks what loyal voters should do next. The episode is a literary warning in plain form. It will speak to supporters who fear their win was stolen by the very swamp they fought. The warning lands harder for its calm tone.
podcast-tuckercarlson-s2T5ZNdsQrU:
Actor Charlie Sheen tells his craziest Hollywood stories to Tucker Carlson and explains why he rejects the official story of 9/11. Sheen, once TV's highest-paid star, lived a public meltdown before a quieter recovery. The bad boy holds court here in full, winning form.

Sheen recounts the wild years, the famous rants, and the cost of that fame. He lays out the questions that made him doubt the official account of the attacks. Carlson, a friend, draws out both the comedy and the candor. Amused and nostalgic viewers get a survivor of celebrity telling it his way.
the-dock-and-the-scaffold-the-manchester:
The Dock and the Scaffold joins two tales of Irish revolt: the Manchester tragedy and the cruise of the Jacknell. Its first pages show Manchester on the morning of November 23, 1867, when crowds of all ranks streamed through frosty streets toward New Bailey Prison. Burghers, clerks, pale mill hands, and the poor of the lanes all pressed the same way.

Three Irishmen faced hanging that day for a rescue in which a police sergeant died. The book mixes court scenes, scaffold scenes, and a sea tale of a Fenian rescue ship. It pleads the patriot cause in strong terms.
the-outdoor-girls-in-the-saddle-or-the-g: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls in the Saddle, or The Girl Miner of Gold Run, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. Hope is billed as author of The Outdoor Girls at Wild Rose Lodge, the Moving Picture Girls, and the Bobbsey Twins. The series list shows the first five Outdoor Girls volumes, from Deepdale to Florida.
the-royal-road-to-health-or-the-secret-o: All that is present here is a Project Gutenberg header for The Royal Road to Health, naming C. A. Tyrrell as its author. The pages shown are the project's standard legal and fundraising notices, with their warnings about changing copyright laws and their appeal for donations. No title page, contents, preface or chapter of Tyrrell's book itself appears, so nothing about its health advice, arguments or structure can be described from what is preserved here.
the-treasure-of-the-incas-a-story-of-adv:
G. A. Henty's Treasure of the Incas, a story of adventure in Peru, opens with his preface to the original edition on the lost Inca hoards. The Spaniards tortured the natives entrusted with the secret and made two or three discoveries, Henty says, but those finds were surely a small part of the missing treasure. For years the occupiers spared no pains and hesitated at no cruelty in hunting hidden wealth. One boat laden with treasure sailed and was generally supposed lost in a storm.

Legends tell that Peruvians fleeing east founded a great city beyond the forests, still occupied by their descendants, in country never explored because the tribes are hostile. Henty promises his two heroes will penetrate the treasure-ship's mystery. He also vouches that his picture of Peru's confusion, misrule, and civil wars is true to the period, history underwriting the adventure as usual with Henty.
the-treaty-of-the-european-union-maastri:
Signed on 7 February 1992, the Treaty on European Union, known as the Maastricht Treaty, is presented here with a contents list that maps its seven titles. Common provisions come first, then amendments to the treaties establishing the European Community, the Coal and Steel Community, and the Atomic Energy Community. Later titles cover a common foreign and security policy, cooperation in justice and home affairs, and final provisions, followed by protocols and declarations.

The opening names the heads of state and government who signed, from the King of the Belgians and the Queen of Denmark to the Queen of the United Kingdom. Their stated resolve is to mark a new stage in European integration begun with the European Communities. This founding document created the European Union and set the road toward the euro, making it essential reading in modern European history.
